issues.title: Accept IFTTT triggers as a hub event source
issues.body:
> Backlog placeholder, filed on 2026-09-25 at the owner's request. It holds the idea until it is clarified and defined. It does not authorize implementation, installation or device changes.

### Outcome

IFTTT triggers become normalized hub events that owner-approved rules can map to moments. Examples are arriving home, sunset, a voice-assistant phrase or a phone button widget.

### Starting points

- IFTTT's "make a web request" action needs a reachable URL, and ADR 0006 keeps services on loopback. Preferred route: IFTTT posts to a secret relay topic (for example ntfy) that the hub subscribes to outbound, so there is still no inbound listener.
- Each event gets a stable ID so duplicates are removed. Relay replays and hub restarts never trigger a moment.
- The hub sets the moment's `start` when the event arrives, not from IFTTT's timestamp. The contract drops moments more than 60 s late.
- Accept only an allowlisted set of event kinds and ignore any free text in the payload.
- IFTTT never commands devices directly. For example, the IFTTT LIFX service must not be used, because it would add a second writer.

- Which trigger to start with, since that decides whether this is worth doing.

issues.title: Drive agent sessions from the Steam Deck: a story launcher, tmux and a controller layout
issues.body:
> Filed 2026-09-25 at the owner's request from the Steam Deck planning session. It defines scope; it does not authorize launching agent sessions, installing software on the Deck or changing personal settings. Delivering the launcher launches nothing; only the owner's explicit command does.

### Outcome and real setup

From the Deck, the owner picks a story and starts its recommended session on the WSL host with one short command, then steers it with the controller. The Deck is a terminal to the PC, not a second agent host: the repositories, the hub and the device writers stay where they are. Setup: mosh or SSH from the Deck to WSL (#378's network check covers SSH), tmux on WSL (3.6 is installed), Claude Code and the Codex CLI on WSL (both installed), Decky Terminal or Konsole on the Deck, and a Steam Input layout. Excluded: a hub dispatch route and task inbox (#204, #205), Codex Desktop targeting (#199), the Decky overlay (#382) and voice.

### Smallest useful implementation

- **Launcher** `docs/work-guide/work/start_story.py`, beside the guide tooling it reuses: `start_story.py H201 --host claude|codex [--cheaper] [--dry-run]`. It reads the live issue with `story_sections.read_issue`, parses the story's Execution recommendation with `recommendations.read`, and takes the saved prompt for the host (the cheaper one when asked). A story whose recommendation state is not `recommended` is refused with its missing input printed. It creates `.local/worktrees/gh-<n>` on a new branch from a freshly fetched `main`, following the global `.local/` rule, and opens a tmux window named `H<n>` in a session named `bunny` that runs `claude "<prompt>"` or `codex "<prompt>"` with the recommended model flag where the CLI supports one. Commands are built as argument vectors, never shell strings. One story, one window: an existing window for the key is selected, not duplicated. `--dry-run` prints the prompt and the commands and changes nothing.
- **Controller layout** as personal setup, described in a short docs/development.md note: D-pad to arrows, A to Enter, B to Escape, X to `y`, Y to `n`, the shoulder buttons to previous and next tmux window, a trigger to Ctrl+C, a touch menu for `/clear`, `/remote-control` and `tmux ls`, the trackpad as a mouse and the on-screen keyboard for text. The hub stores nothing about it.
- **Steering from a browser.** In a running Claude session, `/remote-control` lets claude.ai/code in the Deck's browser continue that session while execution and approvals stay on the PC; the note links Anthropic's Remote Control page. The Codex equivalent is #199's question.
- **Visibility.** With #367 installed, the launched Claude session appears on the Pixoo, the Nanoleaf and B.U.N.N.Y. Codex CLI rows need its hooks, which the provider matrix lists as live-unverified.

Dependencies: none required for the launcher. Preferred order: #378 before the Deck trial, so SSH to WSL is settled. Related: #367, #252 (the saved prompts), #201 (the mission map as the picker).

### Behavior and protections to preserve

- The launcher never edits an issue or its recommendation, never launches a story that is not `recommended`, and never starts a second window for the same story.
- Worktrees live under `.local/worktrees`, never in the main checkout; the launcher runs `git check-ignore` before creating `.local/`.
- Source delivery of the launcher launches no session (AGENTS.md); an owner command does.
- Prompt text stays on the PC. The Deck shows the owner's own terminal over SSH; nothing enters the shared feed or the public guide.

### Observable acceptance and planned evidence

Delivery target: source (the launcher, its tests and the docs note). The tmux session, the SSH setup and the Steam Input layout are the owner's personal setup, recorded as such.

- [ ] **AC1.** Unit tests with fixture bodies: prompt selection by host and cheaper start; refusal on `insufficient`, stale and unassessed states with the reason printed; window naming and de-duplication; `--dry-run` output; argv construction for `claude` and `codex` with a prompt containing quotes and backticks; a fake tmux and a fake `gh` so no session, branch or network call happens in tests.
- [ ] **AC2.** One real launch on the WSL host by the owner: the window opens, the CLI starts with the saved prompt, and the session appears in B.U.N.N.Y. when #367 is installed.
- [ ] **AC3.** A layout trial on the Deck: the owner drives one approval (`y` or `n`) and one window switch; recorded as personal setup, not a hub claim.
- [ ] **AC4.** `python3 docs/work-guide/work/test_maintenance.py` and the guide checks pass; independent Standards and Specification reviews; current-head and merged-revision CI.

### Meaningful deferrals

- A hub dispatch route and the task inbox: #204 and #205. This launcher is offered on #199 as the first adapter candidate because it takes a story key and a host, not arbitrary commands.
- Voice input on the Deck: Wispr has no Linux client and Remote Control documents no dictation; revisit under #47.
- A "level select" in the Decky overlay: after #382.
- Codex Desktop targeting: #199.

### Work assessment

Planning assessment, 2026-09-25; the planning session's reasoning setting is unknown. Complexity: low; a script over existing parsers, git worktree and tmux, with fakes for both. Uncertainty: medium; the two CLIs' initial-prompt and model flags need a check, and the Deck terminal path waits on #378's reachability answer. Impact: medium; it starts real agent sessions that write branches, bounded by the saved prompt and the owner's explicit command. Readiness: ready for the launcher; the Deck trial follows #378.

issues.title: Let the Steam Deck play moments through rumble and an overlay toast
issues.body:
> Backlog placeholder, filed 2026-09-25 at the owner's request from the Steam Deck planning session. It holds the idea until #382's spike answers its questions. It does not authorize implementation, installation or device operations.

### Outcome

A moment can reach the Deck: an attention ping while the owner plays becomes a short controller rumble and a toast in the overlay, and a celebrate moment a different pattern. The Deck becomes a moment-capable device under contract 1.1, declaring its moods, without any device-specific code in the hub (ADR 0006).

### Starting points

- The Deck declares `moods` such as `attention` and `celebrate`, a short duration limit and no status coverage, and translates each mood into a rumble pattern and a toast. Return to base is trivial: the rumble ends. Precedence: an attention ping wins over a flourish; nothing plays while the Deck is suspended.
- Transport is the open question. The hub calls controllers; the Deck sits behind #378's tunnel. Either a reverse tunnel lets the hub reach a controller v1 endpoint the plugin serves, or a `deck` controller inside `apps/local-controllers` (the single-writer pattern from #289) owns the queue and pushes to the plugin over the tunnel. The second fits the existing pattern; #382's spike decides.
- Whether Decky exposes controller haptics to a plugin is unverified; the toast alone is the fallback.

### Protections

- One writer for the Deck as a device; the plugin never becomes a status authority.
- Moments stay transient and the Deck never blocks another device (ADR 0006).
- Nothing plays while the Deck is suspended or the overlay is closed and haptics are unavailable; a missed window is dropped, not queued.

- #382 (the plugin), #335 (the shared moment sender), #292 (contract 1.1, closed), #294 (personas), #295 (agent proposals).

issues.title: Put B.U.N.N.Y. on the Steam Deck: a Decky overlay for agent attention and Deck-side game events
issues.body:
> Filed 2026-09-25 at the owner's request from the Steam Deck planning session. It defines scope; it does not authorize implementation, installation on the Deck, credential creation or device operations.

### Outcome and real setup

While a game runs, the Deck's Quick Access menu shows the same session rows as the Pixoo Monitor tab: which agents are active, which need attention, with an Acknowledge button. The Deck also reports what it observes to the hub's Steam source (#379): app launch and exit, achievement and screenshot notifications, battery level and AC state (which is how docking shows), and suspend and resume. Setup: the owner's Deck with Decky Loader, the SSH tunnel and Deck credential from #378, and the installed hub. Excluded: starting or steering agent sessions (#384, #205), moments played on the Deck (#383), and any control of the Deck's own system settings.

### Smallest useful implementation

- **Package** `apps/steam-deck` in this monorepo (ADR 0003), built from the Decky plugin template: a React and TypeScript frontend on `@decky/ui` and `@decky/api`, and a Python backend. Node 24 build; the deploy loop is the template's rsync over SSH to `~/homebrew/plugins` on the Deck followed by a `plugin_loader` restart, run from WSL and recorded in the package README.
- **Hub access.** The backend talks to `http://127.0.0.1:8788` on the Deck and assumes #378's tunnel is up; when it is not, the overlay shows "hub unreachable" and nothing retries beyond the next poll. The Deck credential lives in `DECKY_PLUGIN_SETTINGS_DIR` with mode 0600 and is entered once through the plugin's settings view.
- **Overlay.** While the Quick Access menu is open, poll `GET /api/monitor/v1/sessions?snapshotVersion=1.1` every few seconds and render provider, owner-chosen label, activity and attention per row; stale evidence renders as stale. Acknowledge posts the monitor command with the server-issued request ID, once per press.
- **Deck adapter.** The frontend registers `SteamClient.GameSessions.RegisterForAppLifetimeNotifications`, `RegisterForAchievementNotification` and `RegisterForScreenshotNotification`, and `SteamClient.System.RegisterForBatteryStateChanges`, `RegisterForOnSuspendRequest` and `RegisterForOnResumeFromSuspend`. The backend posts each as one typed observation to a new hub route `POST /api/steam/v1/observations`, which is #379's push adapter: it accepts the Deck credential's `control` scope, validates a small typed body, rate-limits and never touches the monitor ingest route. A non-Steam shortcut reports `appId: 0` and no name.

Dependencies: #378 (reachability and the credential) and #379 (the source and its observation model) are required inputs. Preferred order: #367 (Claude producer on WSL), so Claude rows appear beside Codex rows. Related: #364 (shared session alias).

### Behavior and protections to preserve

- Session titles and project names (#424), and the latest prompt and agent response (#425), may reach the Deck. Credentials and tokens stay out.
- Acknowledge is not read evidence and clears nothing but the notice, as the agent-state package defines.
- The credential stays on the Deck outside Git; the plugin never gains `ingest`, `admin`, playback or MCP.
- One state owner: the overlay caches presentation and is never a status authority. The plugin sends no device command.
- A Deck that is off, asleep or unreachable changes nothing for agents, hooks or devices (fail open).

### Observable acceptance and planned evidence

Delivery target: source (the package, tests and README); one deploy to the owner's Deck on explicit request; physical acceptance recorded separately. The overlay is a B.U.N.N.Y. surface outside the guide, so the current candidate needs explicit owner approval before merge.

- [ ] **AC1.** Against a fake hub, the overlay renders rows from a fixture snapshot, marks stale evidence, shows the unreachable state, and Acknowledge posts exactly once with the request ID.
- [ ] **AC2.** Against a fake `SteamClient`, each registered event produces one typed observation with the app ID and no name; a shortcut with app ID 0 is reported as 0.
- [ ] **AC3.** The backend stores the credential with mode 0600, never logs it, and bounds retries.
- [ ] **AC4.** The hub's observations route rejects a missing or wrong-scope credential, an oversized body and a burst over the rate limit, with hub tests.
- [ ] **AC5.** On the owner's Deck: a game launch appears as `game.started` in the hub's Steam snapshot within one poll, and a Codex attention row is visible in the overlay during a game. Evidence: a Deck screenshot and the hub snapshot, outside Git.
- [ ] **AC6.** Independent Standards and Specification reviews; current-head and merged-revision CI.

### Meaningful deferrals

- The plugin owning its SSH tunnel: manual tunnel from #378 until this proves useful. Consequence: the owner starts the tunnel before the overlay works.
- Moments on the Deck (rumble, toast): #383.
- A "level select" for stories in the overlay: revisit after #384's launcher exists.
- Deck brightness, TDP or power control: excluded; the Deck owns them.

### Work assessment

Planning assessment, 2026-09-25; the planning session's reasoning setting is unknown. Complexity: high; a new runtime on a new host in two languages, a deploy loop and a new hub route. Uncertainty: high; the `SteamClient` registrations, the plugin's fetch path and the credential handling are unverified on the owner's Deck. Impact: medium; a control-scoped credential lives on the Deck and is recoverable by replacement. Readiness: blocked by #378 and #379. A spike that builds the template, deploys it and logs the lifetime, achievement, battery and suspend events is the first step once the owner grants Deck access.

**Policy update (2026-09-25):** the owner retired the rule that kept titles, project names, prompts, transcripts and paths out of shared data (#424). Credentials and tokens stay excluded. This story's text was updated to match.

issues.title: Run event-triggered routines so a game session sets the desk look and hands it back
issues.body:
> Filed 2026-09-25 at the owner's request from the Steam Deck planning session. It defines scope; it does not authorize implementation, installation or device operations.

### Outcome and real setup

An owner-approved rule maps an event to an ordered list of typed device actions, the same list #359 gives weekly routines. The first use is a game session: on `game.started`, desk preset Free, a Nanoleaf animation in a palette, a Pixoo Media playlist and a LIFX color; on `game.ended`, desk preset Work. That is the persistent session look that a transient moment cannot give (ADR 0006), so the room stays in game colors while the owner plays and returns to status when they stop. Setup: the installed hub with its registered controllers, the #358 rules store, the #359 executor and the #67 desk-preset route. Excluded: new device command kinds, a rule editor UI (#360), and moments (#358 already covers them).

### Smallest useful implementation

- **Rule kind** `event-routine` on the #358 store. Trigger: an event kind, optionally narrowed by source alias and, for Steam, an app ID allowlist. Action: #359's ordered action list with its per-action mode preconditions.
- **Execution** through #359's executor, with its busy rule (one occurrence per rule in flight, later ones logged `busy` and dropped), its `skipped: mode` handling, its log entries, no retry and no catch-up after downtime.
- **Pairing.** A rule may name an ending event kind whose occurrence runs a second action list, so start and end live in one rule. Each list is explicit and runs independently; there is no saved baseline or automatic restoration (#67).
- **Palette.** An action's palette may be a literal or `from-app-art`, which the executor resolves at run time from the dominant colors of the current app's catalog artwork (#379), falling back to the literal. The palette is the only thing derived from the game.
- **Coexistence.** A moment rule (#358) and an event routine may match the same event. Moments are arbitrated and handed to the sender first; the routine runs after. Quiet hours block an event routine unless the rule opts in, default off.

Dependencies: #358 (store and intake), #359 (action list, preconditions, executor and log) and #67 (the desk-preset route) are required inputs. #379 is required only for the `from-app-art` palette and the Steam trigger; any source's event can trigger a routine.

### Behavior and protections to preserve

- A device's selected mode changes only through an explicit desk-preset action the owner put in the rule (ADR 0005, #45). Content actions stay in Free or Media.
- One writer per device through its owning controller; the hub routes typed intents only.
- Existing tickets, revisions, generations, receipts and admission limits; `sent` is transport evidence only.
- Restarts, reconnects and replay never run a routine (#358, #359).
- Rules and the log hold event kinds, app IDs, device aliases and receipts; game, session and task titles may be stored. No credentials or tokens.

### Observable acceptance and planned evidence

Delivery target: source-only. Enabling a rule on the owner's installed hub and any visible change on the physical devices are separately authorized steps.

- [ ] **AC1.** Against fake controllers, a `game.started` rule runs desk preset Free, then the animation, then the playlist, in order, with one receipt each; the paired `game.ended` list runs desk preset Work.
- [ ] **AC2.** The same event matching both a moment rule and an event routine hands the moment to the sender once and runs the routine once, in that order.
- [ ] **AC3.** A content action whose device is in Monitor is skipped with `skipped: mode` and zero device writes; a second occurrence during a still-settling run logs `busy`; quiet hours block the routine unless opted in.
- [ ] **AC4.** `from-app-art` derives a palette from a fixture image and falls back to the literal when the catalog has no artwork.
- [ ] **AC5.** Restart with events delivered before shutdown runs nothing; issue-linked OpenSpec change; hub tests; independent Standards and Specification reviews; current-head and merged-revision CI.

- A Tidbyt "now playing" game card: Tidbyt declares no controller v1 capability today, so it needs its own runner story like #38. Consequence: the Tidbyt keeps showing status during a game.

issues.title: Read the PC's Steam client as a second game-session adapter
issues.body:
> Filed 2026-09-25 at the owner's request from the Steam Deck planning session. It defines scope; it does not authorize implementation, installation or Windows changes.

### Outcome and real setup

When the owner plays on the Windows PC, the Steam source (#379) sees the session from the local Steam client without waiting for the Web API poll. The adapter reads from WSL only: the registry value `HKCU\Software\Valve\Steam\RunningAppID` through `reg.exe` interop (readable from this WSL host on 2026-09-25; it reads 0 while idle) and Steam's `logs/gameprocess_log.txt` under `/mnt/c`, whose `AppID <n> adding PID <m>` lines MoonDeck Buddy already parses. No Windows service, no Steam configuration change. Excluded: play on the Deck (#382), launching games, and non-Steam shortcuts beyond reporting app ID 0.

### Smallest useful implementation

- An in-process adapter in the hub's `steam` source, enabled by a private configuration flag with the Steam install path. It polls the registry value every few seconds and tails the process log for start and stop lines, and reports `{adapter: "pc", appId, running, observedAt}` to the source's merge (#379).
- Why both: Valve's open issue steam-for-linux#9672 reports that the new client leaves `RunningAppID` at 0 on Linux; Windows is unverified. The log gives starts and process exits; the registry gives a cheap confirmation when it works. The first step is a read-only format check on the owner's PC that records what each signal does on the new client.
- Interop failure (`reg.exe` missing, `/mnt/c` unmounted, log unreadable) marks the adapter stale in the source snapshot; the source and the hub keep running.

Dependencies: #379 (the source and its observation model). Preferred order: after #379's AC1 privacy check, so the owner knows which adapter covers PC play.

### Behavior and protections to preserve

- Read-only access to the registry value and the log; no Steam file is written or locked.
- No Windows path, username or game name in events or hub logs; the app ID is the payload.
- The adapter never launches, focuses or closes a game.
- A stale or failed adapter never ends a session another adapter still sees (#379).

### Observable acceptance and planned evidence

Delivery target: source-only; enabling the adapter on the installed hub is a separate explicit step.

- [ ] **AC1.** The format check is recorded in the story: the registry value and the log lines observed on the owner's PC for one game start and stop on the current Steam client.
- [ ] **AC2.** Fake registry output and a fixture log drive the adapter in tests: a start line produces one running observation, the matching exit line one stopped observation, a rotated or truncated log does not replay old lines, and an unparsable line is skipped and counted.
- [ ] **AC3.** With interop unavailable, the adapter reports stale within its freshness window and the source snapshot shows it; no exception escapes.
- [ ] **AC4.** Events and logs contain no path or username; hub tests and independent Standards and Specification reviews; current-head and merged-revision CI.

### Meaningful deferrals

- A Windows-native helper or the Steam client's local IPC: not needed while the log and registry suffice; revisit if the format check finds neither reliable.
- Sunshine prep commands as the PC streaming signal: see #379's deferral.

### Work assessment

Planning assessment, 2026-09-25; the planning session's reasoning setting is unknown. Complexity: low; one poller and one log tail behind the existing adapter interface. Uncertainty: medium; the registry value's reliability on the current Windows client and the exact log lines are unverified until the format check. Impact: low; read-only local reads whose worst failure is a missed or late observation. Readiness: blocked by #379; the format check is ready now as a read-only step.

issues.title: Add a Steam event source that merges game sessions from several adapters, starting with the Web API
issues.body:
> Filed 2026-09-25 at the owner's request from the Steam Deck planning session. It defines scope; it does not authorize implementation, installation, account changes or device operations.

### Outcome and real setup

The hub knows when the owner starts and stops playing a Steam game, on the Deck or the PC, and when an achievement unlocks, as normalized events for #358 rules and for event-triggered routines (#381). One source module owns the account's game-session state and merges observations from several adapters, each with its own freshness: the Steam Web API poll (this story), the PC's Steam client (#380), the Deck itself (#382) and, if the owner ever installs Sunshine, its prep commands (deferred below). Setup: the installed hub, the owner's Steam account and a Web API key in private configuration. No inbound access. Excluded: Rich Presence (no web read path), friends' activity, and any device command.

### Smallest useful implementation

- **Source module** `steam` in the hub, beside playback: a private configuration block with the owner's SteamID64 (a neutral ID), the Web API key, the poll interval (default 30 s) and an optional app allowlist. Missing configuration disables the source and the hub still starts.
- **Observation model.** Every adapter reports `{adapter, appId, running, observedAt}` and an optional typed detail (achievement name, playtime). The source keeps one session state per account: idle, or running `appId` since `startedAt`, with the adapters that currently see it and each adapter's last observation. A session starts when any adapter reports running. It ends when every adapter that reported it reports stopped or goes stale beyond its own freshness window. Conflicting app IDs from two adapters are logged and the later observation wins. No adapter is authoritative; the merged state is.
- **Events** through the #358 intake, each with a stable ID: `game.started` and `game.ended` (`steam:<appId>:<startedAt>`), `achievement.unlocked` (`steam:<appId>:<apiname>`) and `playtime.milestone` (`steam:<appId>:<hours>`, one per whole hour of the current session). Events carry the kind, the source alias `steam`, the app ID and the owner's label for that app when one exists. No game name reaches the intake, a device or the moment log.
- **Web API adapter.** `ISteamUser/GetPlayerSummaries` for `gameid` at the poll interval. While a session runs, `ISteamUserStats/GetPlayerAchievements` for that app every few polls, diffed against the last unlock set. `IPlayerService/GetRecentlyPlayedGames` once per session end for playtime. Backoff on errors, well under Valve's 100,000 calls per day. Restart never re-emits: the source persists the last session and unlock set in the hub's private store and seeds from them.
- **Private app catalog.** App ID to name and artwork URL (`https://cdn.cloudflare.steamstatic.com/steam/apps/<appId>/library_600x900.jpg`, unauthenticated) in the private store, for the owner's UI and for palette derivation in #381. It is never exported and never enters the shared feed.
- **Read route** `GET /api/steam/v1/snapshot` with `read` scope: the merged session state, per-adapter freshness and the catalog row for the current app.

Dependencies: #358 (the event intake; the source can be built and tested against a fake intake, but no rule fires without it). Preferred order: #293 first, so the two pollers share one shape. Sibling sources: #293, #298, #352.

### Behavior and protections to preserve

- Services stay on loopback; the source makes outbound HTTPS to the Steam Web API only.
- The key stays in private configuration outside Git; logs never print it or the SteamID.
- Events carry kind, alias, app ID and an owner-chosen label: game titles, friends and chat may be included.
- Restarts, reconnects and replay never emit events (#358).
- Existing monitoring, controller, playback and MCP behavior is unchanged. The source sends no device command.

### Observable acceptance and planned evidence

Delivery target: source-only. Enabling the source on the installed hub with the owner's key is a separate explicit step.

- [ ] **AC1.** Privacy check recorded first: with the owner's key and current profile settings, `GetPlayerSummaries` returns `gameid` while a game runs on the Deck, or it does not and the story records which profile setting the owner changed. Valve documents the own-key privacy exemption for the playtime methods only, so this is a real check, not an assumption.
- [ ] **AC2.** Fake adapter tests: one adapter running then stopped produces exactly one started and one ended event with the same session ID; two adapters seeing the same app produce one session; one adapter going stale while another still sees the game keeps the session; conflicting app IDs are logged and resolved to the later observation.
- [ ] **AC3.** The Web API adapter against a fake HTTP server: poll cadence, backoff on 429 and 5xx, one `achievement.unlocked` per new unlock, and a restart with a persisted session emits nothing until the state changes.
- [ ] **AC4.** Events reaching a fake #358 intake carry no game name; the private catalog holds it; the snapshot route enforces `read` scope.
- [ ] **AC5.** Issue-linked OpenSpec change, hub tests, independent Standards and Specification reviews, current-head and merged-revision CI.

### Meaningful deferrals

- Sunshine or Apollo prep commands as an adapter: revisit when the owner installs Sunshine on the PC. Until then PC streaming sessions are seen by the PC adapter (#380) only.
- Friends online and Rich Presence: not read yet because the Web API offers no read path, not for privacy. Add them when an adapter can read them.
- A B.U.N.N.Y. widget for the current game: after #287's inventory. The snapshot route is enough for the launcher and the Deck overlay.

### Work assessment

Planning assessment, 2026-09-25; the planning session's reasoning setting is unknown. Complexity: medium; a poller, a multi-adapter reducer with freshness, persistence and one route. Uncertainty: medium; whether the owner's key sees the summary game fields is a bounded check, and the intake shape follows #358. Impact: medium; a wrong session fires or misses an owner-approved moment, and nothing writes to a device directly. Readiness: blocked by #358's intake. AC1's privacy check is ready as soon as the owner creates a key.

**Policy update (2026-09-25):** the owner retired the rule that kept titles, project names, prompts, transcripts and paths out of shared data (#424). Credentials and tokens stay excluded. This story's text was updated to match. Steam friends and chat are also allowed.

issues.title: Reach the hub from the Steam Deck through an SSH tunnel
issues.body:
> Filed 2026-09-25 at the owner's request from the Steam Deck planning session. It defines scope and records a route decision the owner still has to make. It does not authorize implementation, installation, credential creation, firewall changes or device operations.

### Outcome and real setup

The owner opens B.U.N.N.Y. and the hub's read and control routes from the Steam Deck on the home LAN, while the installed hub (`codex-nanoleaf-monitor.service`, loopback port 8788 in WSL) keeps its loopback-only listener and its Host, Origin and `Sec-Fetch-Site` checks unchanged. This is the reassessment that #276 asks for before any second device reaches the hub: the Deck is that second device. Excluded: internet or phone access (#47, #203), a LAN bind for the hub, a second operator, and the Decky plugin itself (#382).

### Smallest useful implementation

- **Route.** An SSH tunnel from the Deck to the WSL host that forwards the hub port to the Deck's own loopback (`ssh -L 8788:127.0.0.1:8788 <wsl-host>`). The Deck's browser opens `http://127.0.0.1:8788/`, so the existing Host and Origin checks pass with no code change, and the trusted-loopback sign-in from #276, once installed, signs the Deck's browser in exactly as it signs in the PC's. Until #276 is installed, the manual token form works over the tunnel.
- **Reaching WSL from the LAN.** WSL2's default NAT accepts no inbound LAN connections. The first step is a bounded check of three candidates: a Windows port proxy to the WSL `sshd`, WSL mirrored networking, or Tailscale inside WSL with the tunnel over the tailnet. Record the working one in `apps/hub/SETUP.md` with the firewall rule it needs; the owner adds that rule explicitly (AGENTS.md: agents change no firewall settings).
- **Deck credential.** For machine clients on the Deck (#382), one dedicated machine credential created with the hub README's "Create a credential" procedure, scoped to `read` and `control` on the configured device aliases and the monitor commands, with no `ingest`, `admin`, playback or MCP grant. Revocation is the existing credential replacement.
- **Documentation.** A "Steam Deck" subsection in `apps/hub/SETUP.md`: the SSH key on the Deck, the tunnel command, the bookmark and the revocation steps, plus a Deck client row in the README's credential table. No hub code change is expected; if the check finds one is needed, for example a Host alias, it is named here before implementation.

Dependencies: none required. Preferred order: #276 (trusted-loopback sign-in) before daily use, so the Deck needs no token form. Related: #47, #203, #205.

### Behavior and protections to preserve

- The loopback-only listener, exact Host and Origin checks, the `Sec-Fetch-Site` rule and the `X-Pixoo-Request` header on every write.
- Machine credentials stay digest-only in private configuration; nothing on the Deck holds `ingest`, `admin`, playback or MCP scopes.
- Browser-session retirement from #244; one state owner and one writer per device.
- Assurance lost, stated plainly: with #276's option on, any program on the Deck that can reach the Deck's loopback while the tunnel is up can issue the same read and control commands as the owner's browser. The devices are lights and displays, and the tunnel is up only while the owner's SSH session is. Reassess again before a third device or an operator other than the owner.

### Observable acceptance and planned evidence

Delivery target: a recorded owner decision, the network check result and a SETUP.md section; installation on the Deck and the PC by the owner on explicit request.

- [ ] **AC1.** The network check records which of the three candidates works on the owner's PC and Deck, with the exact commands and the firewall rule it needs. A candidate that fails is recorded as failed, not assumed.
- [ ] **AC2.** With the tunnel up, `http://127.0.0.1:8788/` on the Deck shows the dashboard. The existing hub tests for Host, Origin and `Sec-Fetch-Site` pass unchanged, and a request carrying a LAN Host header is still refused.
- [ ] **AC3.** A Deck-scoped credential is created, used for one read and one monitor acknowledge over the tunnel, then replaced; the old digest is refused with HTTP 401.
- [ ] **AC4.** SETUP.md documents the route, the bookmark and the revocation, and the README credential table gains the Deck client row.

Evidence: the check transcript and screenshots under `.local/evidence/` outside Git, with addresses redacted.

### Meaningful deferrals

- Tailscale as the long-term route for use away from home: revisit when #47 is refined. Consequence: the tunnel works only on the LAN.
- A LAN bind for the hub: rejected, because it widens the listener for every client. Consequence: each new device needs its own tunnel.
- Starting the tunnel automatically on Deck boot: a manual `ssh` command until the Decky plugin (#382) owns its connection.

### Work assessment

Planning assessment, 2026-09-25; the planning session's reasoning setting is unknown. Complexity: low; a tunnel, one credential and documentation, with no hub code expected. Uncertainty: medium; WSL2 inbound reachability from the LAN and the tunneled page's sign-in path are bounded checks with a way to answer them. Impact: high; it is an authorization boundary change that adds a second device able to command lights and displays, even though the diff is small. Readiness: needs the owner's decision on the route (the tunnel is proposed; Tailscale and a LAN bind are the alternatives), then ready as a bounded check.

issues.title: Estimate per-room coverage for each Roborock run from its map
issues.body:
### Outcome and real setup

Each run on the B.U.N.N.Y. Roborock page from #376 lists the rooms it covered, with the estimated area vacuumed and mopped in each room and the share of that room's floor, labeled as an estimate. A room summary shows when each room was last cleaned and how often in the last 30 days.

Setup: the same hub, vacuum and private run store as #376.

Excluded: drawing the map in B.U.N.N.Y., coverage for runs without a captured map, and any device contact beyond #376's collector.

### Smallest useful implementation

The robot reports no per-room time or area; a run record has only totals, and its `cleaned_area` equals `area`. The robot doesn't return past-run maps: `get_clean_record_map` gets no reply. The current map from `get_map_v1` carries the rooms, the vacuum path and a separate mop path, and #376 captures it when each run ends.

1. **Room pixel masks.** [`vacuum-map-parser-roborock`](https://github.com/PiotrMachowski/Python-package-vacuum-map-parser-roborock) 0.1.5, which `python-roborock` bundles, decodes this model's map, but it keeps only each room's bounding box. Read each room's floor pixels from the raw map's image block, which the parser reads but doesn't keep.
2. **Coverage.** Draw the vacuum path and the mop path onto the map grid, each at a fixed width, and intersect them with each room's pixels. The widths are named constants, recorded in the README. Report vacuumed and mopped m² and the percentage of each room's floor.
3. **Room names.** Use the names from #376's room mapping, stored with each run so that renaming or re-mapping rooms doesn't rewrite past runs.
4. **When to compute.** Compute when a run's map is stored, and backfill runs that already have a captured map, idempotently. The runs stored on the robot before #376 was installed have no map.
5. **Serve and show.** Add per-run room coverage and the room summary to the `roborock-vacuum` profile as a minor version, and show them on the run detail and the Roborock page.

Dependencies: #376, which provides the captured maps, room mapping, profile and page.

### Behavior and protections to preserve

- Coverage is labeled an estimate everywhere, and the fixed width is documented.
- A run with no captured map, or a map that fails to parse, shows "coverage unknown". The run still shows its totals, and no rooms are invented.
- Raw maps and floor geometry never leave the private store. Responses carry only room names and numbers. Fixtures are hand-built synthetic maps.
- #376's read-only collector and its history are unchanged.

### Observable acceptance and planned evidence

Delivery target: source. Checking against a real run follows #376's installation, on the owner's request.

- Synthetic-map tests cover:
  - room pixels read from a synthetic raw image block;
  - a path inside one room counted only for that room;
  - a path across two rooms split between them;
  - an untouched room showing zero;
  - a mop path counted separately from the vacuum path;
  - an unparseable or missing map reported as unknown;
  - a backfill run twice giving identical results;
  - a room renamed after a run keeping the old name on that run.
- Contract tests cover the profile minor version.
- The owner approves the run detail and room summary UI.
- **When installed:** for one real run, the listed rooms match the rooms the Roborock app's run map shows as cleaned.

### Meaningful deferrals

- **A drawn map or heatmap in B.U.N.N.Y.** Use the app's run map. Revisit on request.
- **Coverage for runs without a captured map.** The runs already on the robot, and any run that ends while the collector is down, show "coverage unknown". The Roborock app shows their maps. No revisit planned; the robot doesn't return past-run maps.
- **"Room not cleaned in N days" alerts.** Revisit with #376's alert deferral, as moments.

## Work assessment

Planning assessment, 2026-09-25, against hub `main` `21583cd`.

- **Complexity: medium.** Room pixel extraction, a geometric estimate for two paths, a backfill and a profile minor version.
- **Uncertainty: medium.** On 2026-09-25 this model's current map decoded with rooms, a vacuum path and a mop path (see comments). Room pixel extraction and the estimate's accuracy remain; the real-run comparison bounds the second.
- **Impact: low.** Derived read-only data; nothing reaches the device.

**Readiness:** blocked on #376.

issues.title: Collect Roborock status and run history and show them in B.U.N.N.Y.
issues.body:
### Outcome and real setup

The owner's Roborock S8 MaxV Ultra gets its own page in B.U.N.N.Y. and appears in `hub_devices` over MCP.

- **Now:** state (docked, cleaning, returning, charging, error), battery %, the current run's time and area, dock status (water tanks, dust bag, dock errors) and consumable wear (main brush, side brush, filter, sensors, dock strainer).
- **Run history:** each run's start, end, duration, area, how it started (app, schedule, dock button, voice), how it finished (completed, stopped, could not continue, positioning failed), error code, obstacles avoided and mop washes.
- **Battery curve:** battery % over time for each run the collector observed.
- **Totals:** lifetime clean time, area, run count and dust collections.

Setup: one operator, the installed hub on the WSL host, the vacuum at an IP the owner supplies, and the owner's existing Roborock app account.

Excluded: sending commands (start, pause, dock, room cleans), per-room coverage (#377), map display and obstacle photos.

### Smallest useful implementation

There is no official Roborock API. [`python-roborock`](https://github.com/Python-roborock/python-roborock), the library the official Home Assistant integration uses, logs in once with the account email and a one-time code to fetch the device's local key. It then reads the robot directly over TCP port 58867. The prior check confirmed local polling. The library also maintains a cloud MQTT subscription, but status pushes were not observed; qualify the observation path before settling cadence. It also blocks its local API while it cannot reach Roborock's servers.

1. **Qualify read-only, at pickup.** With the owner's IP and permission, log in once with a pinned `python-roborock` and read `get_status`, `get_clean_summary`, one `get_clean_record`, `get_consumable`, `get_room_mapping` and the size of one `get_clean_record_map`, locally. The S8 MaxV Ultra is not on the library's documented model list, so record in a comment: model and firmware, which fields are populated, how many past runs the robot keeps, and whether local reads work. Leave out the IP, device ID, tokens, local key and any map content.
2. **Controller service in `controllers/roborock`.** A Python 3.12 process with `python-roborock` pinned by hash in its own virtual environment. A `login` subcommand prompts for the email and code (never on the command line) and writes the session to a mode-600 file outside Git. A mode-600 config names the explicit IP. One lease file keeps a second copy from running.
3. **Collector.** Poll status every 60 s while docked and every 15 s while cleaning or returning. Store battery and state samples for each run. When a run ends, and at startup, read the clean summary, then fetch and store every run record not yet stored, keyed by record ID. Then capture the current map with `get_map_v1` and store it with that run for #377. The robot doesn't answer `get_clean_record_map`, so this is the only way to get a run's map; a run that ends while the collector is down has none. Everything goes in a private SQLite file under `~/.local/state/agent-device-hub/roborock/` on ext4.
4. **Serve it.** Serve controller v1 on loopback with every capability unsupported, as the Tidbyt controller does. Add a read-only `roborock-vacuum` 1.0.0 profile for the status and a paged run history without maps. Use the same token, Origin and Host checks as the local controller host. Read `docs/controller-contract.md` before adding the profile.
5. **Hub and dashboard.** Register the device in the hub, add the profile read route, and add a B.U.N.N.Y. page under [ADR 0007](https://github.com/jimmie-potts/agent-device-hub/blob/main/docs/decisions/0007-bunny-shell.md): status, run list, and run detail with the battery curve.

**Decision needed at pickup:** where the protocol runs. The only maintained implementation is Python, and the local controller host from [#289](https://github.com/jimmie-potts/agent-device-hub/issues/289) is Node. The recommendation is the separate Python service above, registered with the hub like the Pixoo and Nanoleaf services. The alternatives are a Python child process of the #289 host, or Home Assistant under [#11](https://github.com/jimmie-potts/agent-device-hub/issues/11). Home Assistant adds a runtime and uses the same library, but #11 identifies several possible device consumers. Compare total operating cost and observational-only suitability across the selected candidates; no route is adopted here.

Dependencies: none required. This adds the first Python package dependency outside `requirements-contracts.txt`, so coordinate the setup and CI change under `docs/development.md`.

### Behavior and protections to preserve

- **Read-only.** The Roborock app stays the only thing that commands the vacuum. The service sends only an allowlist of read commands, and a test proves it refuses any other command.
- **Explicit target.** Only the configured IP; no LAN discovery or broadcast.
- **Credentials.** The account session and local key live only in the mode-600 file. They never appear in logs, arguments, responses, issues or Git.
- **Private data.** Run history, maps and room names stay in the private SQLite file. Test fixtures are synthetic, not taken from the real vacuum.
- **Truthful freshness.** When the vacuum is unreachable, including while it is offline from the internet, the page shows the last observation and its age, not "docked". A run stored while the collector was down shows no battery curve instead of an invented one. Missing fields show as unknown.
- **Isolation.** A vacuum failure does not affect other devices or the hub.

### Observable acceptance and planned evidence

Delivery target: source, plus the read-only check at pickup. Installation and the real-run comparison need the owner's request.

- The qualification comment records model, firmware, populated fields and history depth, with nothing private.
- Fake-transport tests cover:
  - state mapping and the poll-rate change at run start and end;
  - a run end storing its record once, with no duplicate after a restart or a repeated summary;
  - a run end capturing the current map once and attaching it to that run, and a run found only in the summary stored without a map;
  - battery samples attached to the right run;
  - an unreachable vacuum reported stale with its age;
  - missing fields reported as unknown;
  - a non-allowlisted command refused;
  - config and session files rejected when readable by others or inside a Git checkout.
- Contract tests cover the `roborock-vacuum` profile. With fakes, `hub_devices` lists the vacuum.
- The B.U.N.N.Y. page shows status, runs and a battery curve with fakes. The owner approves the UI under the SDLC UI scope.
- The shared build, type, contract and workflow checks and the hub, MCP and dashboard suites pass, plus a new `test:roborock` suite added to `docs/development.md` and CI.
- **When installed:** one real run's duration and area match the Roborock app's record for that run, within rounding, and the path in its captured map matches that run's map in the app.

### Meaningful deferrals

- **Commands** (start, pause, dock, clean rooms). Use the Roborock app. Revisit when the owner asks. python-roborock#962 reports fan and water mode commands failing on this model.
- **Room coverage.** Owned by #377. This story captures each run's map when the run ends.
- **Map and obstacle photos in B.U.N.N.Y.** Use the app. Revisit on request. Photos are private media.
- **Cloud fallback.** If local reads fail, status is unavailable. Revisit if local reads prove unreliable.
- **Alerts** ("stuck", "dock needs water") on the wall or Tidbyt. Revisit once history works, as moments under [ADR 0006](https://github.com/jimmie-potts/agent-device-hub/blob/main/docs/decisions/0006-hub-moments-and-interludes.md).
- **An MCP tool for run history.** `hub_devices` shows current status. Revisit when an agent needs history.

## Home Assistant comparison — 2026-10-01

The wider [#11](https://github.com/jimmie-potts/agent-device-hub/issues/11) candidate set changes the cost comparison. Compare [HA Roborock](https://www.home-assistant.io/integrations/roborock/) with the dedicated Python proposal before selecting the protocol host.

- [ ] Compare populated status/consumable fields, observation cadence, cloud/account behavior and run/map access. Retain private history, battery curves, run-end map capture and #377; HA entity history alone does not satisfy them.
- [ ] Audit pinned HA/library initialization, updates and map paths for writes. The [qualification handoff](https://github.com/jimmie-potts/agent-device-hub/issues/376#issuecomment-5841483272) warns that MapsTrait can send load_multi_map. Hiding command buttons does not prove observational-only operation.
- [ ] Preserve prior local-read/history/map evidence. Status pushes were not observed; qualify any push path before changing polling. Any required cloud fallback or expanded access needs an owner decision against the current policy.
- [ ] Preserve one private history owner and versioned exports for apartment consumers. No second SQLite reader, new device contact or renewal of prior one-time probe permission is implied.

## Work assessment

HA comparison reassessed on 2026-10-01 against the sources and acceptance above. Complexity/impact and readiness remain; route uncertainty is now high. This adds candidate evidence, not adoption or physical qualification. Reassess on route/host selection or a failed required capability.

Planning assessment, 2026-09-25, against hub `main` `21583cd`.

- **Complexity: medium.** A new service with a polling state machine, a private store, a new profile, a hub route and a dashboard page.
- **Uncertainty: high for route selection.** Protocol host, initialization side effects and cloud-policy compatibility remain unresolved. The first installed run still has to show that the captured path belongs to that run.
- **Impact: medium.** No device writes, but it holds a cloud account session and the device's local key.

**Readiness:** needs clarification on the transport decision above. On 2026-09-25 the owner supplied the vacuum's IP privately and granted the one-time login and the read-only check in step 1.

issues.title: Install the Claude Code producer on the WSL host so Claude sessions reach the shared owner
issues.body:
## Outcome and scope

Claude Code sessions on the WSL host reach the installed shared owner `personal-shared-monitor`, so the Pixoo, Nanoleaf and B.U.N.N.Y. show `claude`/`code` rows beside Codex. Owning repository: agent-device-hub (the setup SDK in `apps/hub/SETUP.md`). Excluded: Windows-native Claude Code, device changes, Pixoo code, and the qualification of session ends, which #312 owns.

Observed on 2026-09-25: the host has producers for Codex CLI (`shared-monitor/cli`) and Codex Desktop (`shared-monitor/desktop`) only. Both `~/.claude/settings.json` and the Windows `settings.json` have an empty `hooks` object, and the owner holds no `claude` sessions. #312 describes "the owner's Claude Code hooks" as part of its setup; they do not exist yet, so #312 depends on this story.

## Acceptance criteria

- A named installation owner runs a reviewed `planSetup` and `applySetup` (SDK, no CLI exists) with: a new receipt directory `shared-monitor/claude`; `target` `~/.claude/settings.json`; source `{provider:'claude', client:'code', hostId:'wsl-ubuntu', sourceId:'claude-code', hook:'SessionStart'}`; the owner's `/api/monitor/v1/events` endpoint on 127.0.0.1:8788; the runtime Node 24 and `bin/monitor-hook.mjs`; no `windowsDistribution`.
- The plan's before/after diff is reviewed privately; unrelated hooks and trust settings survive; the backup and receipt stay outside Git with mode 0600.
- `qualified` starts false. It is set true only after the owner records the installed Claude Code version, the execution path, the trust review and observed event coverage, per SETUP.md.
- With `qualified: true`, one Claude Code session shows as a `claude` row on the Pixoo Monitor tab and B.U.N.N.Y., with SessionStart, UserPromptSubmit, Stop and SessionEnd observed. Claude has no Interrupt event; the record stays uncertain where evidence is missing.
- Removal via `planRemoval` and `removeSetup` restores the settings without touching unrelated entries, and revocation is confirmed with HTTP 401.

## Dependencies

- #8 delivered the reversible setup SDK (closed).
- #312 (qualify Claude Code and Codex CLI ends) depends on this story.
- Related: jimmie-potts/divoom-app-upgrade#87 (row identifiers) and #364 (shared session alias), so Claude rows are distinguishable once they appear.

issues.title: Let the owner arrange the B.U.N.N.Y. home from a widget catalog and keep the layout in the hub
issues.body:
> Filed 2026-09-25 at the owner's direction. It defines scope and acceptance; it does not authorize implementation or installation.

### Outcome and real setup

The owner decides what the B.U.N.N.Y. home shows. From a catalog of every available widget, the owner adds, removes, hides, reorders and resizes widgets on the home grid, keeps a separate arrangement for the phone, and the layout is saved in the hub so it is the same on the PC and the phone. Until this lands, widget placement is a developer decision made in code (#277). Owner direction, 2026-09-25: a highly customizable dashboard to monitor my life, not a fixed component dashboard.

Setup is the installed hub and the owner's browsers on the PC and the phone. One owner, so one saved layout per breakpoint; no accounts, sharing or templates.

### Smallest useful implementation, with dependencies

- **Widget catalog.** Every widget built on the #277 interface registers itself with an ID, a name, a short description, the sizes it supports and the data source it needs (a registered controller alias, a hub route, or an external source from #287). The catalog is the list the owner picks from. A widget whose source is not configured appears in the catalog as unavailable with the reason, following the disabled-control rule from ADR 0005.
- **Edit mode.** One explicit "Edit layout" control on the home page. In edit mode each widget shows move, resize (small, medium, large, from its supported set), hide and remove controls, and an "Add widget" panel lists the catalog. Reorder works by drag and by keyboard (arrow keys move the focused widget one cell; #288's roving grid supplies the focus model). "Done" saves; "Reset to default" restores the built-in arrangement. Outside edit mode the grid behaves exactly as #277 delivers it.
- **Two breakpoints.** One arrangement for the desktop grid and one for the phone column. Editing on either device edits that breakpoint's arrangement. A widget added on one breakpoint is appended to the other so nothing is silently invisible.
- **Storage.** A `layout` record in the hub's private state (`state.sqlite`), versioned, holding per-breakpoint ordered entries of widget ID, size and hidden flag. Read with the dashboard's existing session, written through one typed route with the existing browser-session authentication and `X-Pixoo-Request: 1`. Not `localStorage`, because the layout must follow the owner across devices and survive a browser reset. Unknown widget IDs in a saved layout (a widget removed by a later release) are dropped on read and reported once.
- **Defaults.** The built-in arrangement is #277's approved home grid. A first visit shows it; the owner's first edit creates the saved record.

Dependencies: #277 (widget interface and home grid). #288 for the keyboard focus model; before it, keyboard reorder uses the edit controls on each widget. #287 supplies the catalog ranking and external sources but is not a prerequisite for the mechanism.

### Behavior and protections to preserve

- Edit mode changes layout only. No widget applies a device command while being moved, resized or hidden. The command spy stays at zero in every layout test.
- Every widget renders identically wherever it is placed and at every size it declares (#277). Hiding a widget stops its polling.
- Alert visibility: an attention or failure alert on a device that shows tasks stays visible on the home page even when its widget is hidden, through the existing stats strip or attention inbox. A saved layout cannot suppress a red or yellow alert.
- Keyboard order, focus restoration, reduced motion, axe WCAG 2.1 AA at desktop and 390 px, and no horizontal overflow. Drag has a keyboard equivalent.
- The hub serves only the three dashboard assets under the existing CSP; no inline styles.
- The layout record holds widget IDs, sizes and flags only. No credentials, private paths, labels or content.

### Observable acceptance and planned evidence

- [ ] **AC1.** The catalog lists every registered widget with availability and reason; adding one places it on the grid; removing and hiding behave as named; reset restores the default.
- [ ] **AC2.** Reorder and resize work by drag and by keyboard; the result persists across a page reload and across a hub restart; the desktop and phone arrangements are independent and a widget added on one appears on the other.
- [ ] **AC3.** No layout action sends a controller command; hidden widgets stop polling; an alert on a hidden device widget remains visible on the home page.
- [ ] **AC4.** A saved layout naming an unknown widget ID loads without error, drops the entry and reports it once.
- [ ] **AC5.** Accessibility checks pass in and out of edit mode at desktop and 390 px; explicit human UI approval is recorded in the PR under the SDLC UI approval scope.
- [ ] **AC6.** Issue-linked OpenSpec change for the `unified-dashboard` delta and the layout route; `npm run test:dashboard`, `npm run test:dashboard:browser` and hub tests pass; independent Standards and Specification reviews; current-head and merged-revision CI.

**Delivery target:** source-only. Installing on the owner's host is a separately authorized step.

### Meaningful deferrals

- Several named layouts or extra pages the owner composes: one home layout per breakpoint first. Revisit when the home grid overflows two screens.
- Per-widget settings beyond size (which repository, which calendar, refresh rate): each widget's own story, stored beside the layout entry when needed.
- Sharing, templates or a second user: none; personal project.
- Custom grid cell sizes or free positioning: fixed cells from #277. Revisit if the fixed grid blocks a widget the owner wants.

### Work assessment

Planning assessment, 2026-09-25. Complexity: medium; a catalog registry, an edit mode with drag and keyboard, one persisted record and route. Uncertainty: low to medium; the widget interface must be built first, and the exact sizes depend on the #277 candidate. Impact: low; layout only, with a reset.

**Readiness:** backlog until #277 is merged. **Reassessment triggers:** #277's candidate changing the grid model, or #288 landing first.

Related: #277, #287, #288, #283, #286, #353, #360, #271.

issues.body:
> Backlog placeholder, filed on 2026-09-25 from the Pixoo display-alignment sweep at the owner's request. It holds the idea until it is clarified and defined. It does not authorize implementation, installation or device changes.

### Outcome

Every device that shows agent sessions uses the same short, neutral code for the same session: the Pixoo row, a LIFX Beam zone run, a Nanoleaf Line, a Tidbyt tile and B.U.N.N.Y. all say `T3` for the same task. The owner learns one code per session instead of one per device.

When no label was set, the Pixoo fell back to the first five characters of the session UUID (jimmie-potts/divoom-app-upgrade#87, since changed to the ID's end), so every Codex Desktop session from the same period reads `01A0D+`. issues.title: Add B.U.N.N.Y. Automation widgets and MCP tools for rules and routines
issues.body:
> Child 3 of 3 of #45, filed 2026-09-25. Adds the B.U.N.N.Y. Automation page and MCP tools over the store from #358 and the routines from #359 (see #45 for links).

### Outcome and real setup

The owner inspects, creates, edits, enables, disables and deletes event rules and routines from a B.U.N.N.Y. Automation page, edits the interrupt set and quiet hours there, and reads the automation log. Agents can list rules and routines, read the log, and propose a rule or routine through MCP; a proposal is stored disabled and runs only after the owner enables it (ADR 0004).

Setup is the installed hub, the operator's browser and the agent clients the hub already supports.

### Smallest useful implementation, with dependencies

- **Automation widgets** in `apps/dashboard`, on the #277 widget interface and registered in the widget catalog (#366), composed on an Automation page by default:
  - **Rules and routines**: the list with kind, enabled state, last outcome and next occurrence, with enable, disable and run-now on each row. Sizes medium and large.
  - **Next routines**: the next few occurrences across all routines with their targets. Sizes small and medium. This is the card meant for the home grid.
  - **Automation log**: the paged log. Sizes medium and large.
  - **Interrupt set and quiet hours**: the two editors. Size medium.
  The page follows the B.U.N.N.Y. shell and skin (ADR 0007, #182) and adds a form per kind. The event-rule form offers event kinds from registered sources, moods and classes from each target's declared `moments` capability, and target aliases from registered controllers. The routine form offers local weekdays and `HH:MM` only, with no routine timezone field or selector, and an ordered action list built from each target's declared capabilities, showing the mode precondition per action with its default. Pixoo targets show playlist names and, once #353 is delivered, previews; before that, IDs and names. Interrupt set and quiet hours are edited on the same page. The existing bounded log shows attempted-action results and admission outcomes with their reasons, preserving receipt, not-sent and uncertain meanings alongside blocked/skipped/busy. Do not add missed-run rows, a missed-history display, manual-command auditing or historical reconstruction.
- **Run now** submits once and shows the returned occurrence ID, then reads eventual per-action results through the existing automation log. It does not wait indefinitely for receipts or resubmit a pending/uncertain run. **Enable/disable** uses the existing typed routes and errors. A widget applies nothing while being placed or resized. Leave the existing daily quiet-hours settings intact; do not rebuild them around routine schedules.
- **MCP tools** in `apps/hub`: `automation_list`, `automation_log`, `automation_propose` (creates a disabled rule or routine and returns its ID), `automation_enable` and `automation_disable`. `read` scope for the first two, `control` for the rest. Tools a token's scopes do not cover are left out of the tool list, as the hub already does.
- **Routes.** Reuse the typed routes from #358 and #359; add nothing device-facing.

Dependencies: #358 and #359. #277 for the widget interface. #353 for Pixoo previews in the editor (optional). #182 for the shell. #366 for owner placement on the home grid (optional; the default page works without it).

### Behavior and protections to preserve

- The browser never receives device credentials or private SQLite state; it uses hub routes only.
- Proposing never enables. Only an explicit owner action with `control` scope enables a rule or routine.
- The page creates no writer, no scheduler and no restoration state. Physical effects are scheduled only by the hub process.
- Disabled controls name the missing capability or scope, as #151 and ADR 0005 require.

issues.title: Run weekly scheduled routines through typed device commands with content-mode preconditions
issues.body:
> Child 2 of 3 of https://github.com/jimmie-potts/agent-device-hub/issues/45. Owner-approved scope reduction, September 30, 2026: keep weekly routines and scheduled moments; use the hub host's local clock; remove timezone features and missed-run history. This replaces the earlier timezone/DST, downtime-accounting and manual-history requirements. It changes planning, not delivery status.

### Outcome and real setup

On the owner's one hub installation, enabled routines run an ordered list of typed device actions at selected local times and weekdays, without a conversation or a model call. Examples: start an evening Pixoo playlist, turn a screen off, select a desk preset, or play a scheduled moment.

Use the host's existing local clock. Do not add a timezone field, timezone selector, named-zone conversion, a hard-coded Eastern zone, a timezone library, or custom DST/zone-change behavior. Changing the host's clock configuration is outside this delivery. The routine editor and MCP tools remain https://github.com/jimmie-potts/agent-device-hub/issues/360.

### Smallest useful implementation, with dependencies

- **Rules and clock.** Extend the existing store with `kind:"routine"`, weekly `{days,time}` entries (`HH:MM`) and ordered actions. Use one timer inside the hub and a small executor callable independently of it. Persist rules and minimal duplicate-prevention state, not a durable job queue. Submit only due occurrences to their own routine; use valid bounded IDs, a separate run-now identity and a distinct identity for each action. Edits/disable/delete invalidate pending work. Expose a bounded upcoming-occurrence read.
- **Downtime.** Startup schedules future occurrences only. Do not catch up, resume interrupted actions, enumerate misses, write `missed` rows or reconstruct history. This applies to every outage length. Existing duplicate/replay protection stays.
- **Commands.** Reuse existing guarded power, brightness, media, integration and lighting operations. Obtain fresh request identities/revisions/generations at dispatch; store no credentials or stale request envelopes. Desk presets target #67's configured participant group. Add no device command kinds. Content actions require Pixoo Media or Nanoleaf Free: atomic admission where supported, otherwise a fresh best-effort snapshot check; an unknown required mode means zero command writes. Power/brightness retain mode-independent behavior. Only explicit desk presets may change modes.
- **Execution.** Run actions in order with existing bounds; a failed/unavailable action does not stop the rest. One occurrence per routine may run at a time; overlap logs `busy` and drops. No retries, rollback, restoration baseline or background enforcement. The next occurrence supersedes a manual change, without recording manual-command history.
- **Scheduled moments stay.** `{kind:"moment", mood, durationMs, palette?, targets}` uses #358 arbitration and the real #335 sender as `flourish`, `coversStatus:false`. Preserve existing switch, quiet-hours, global budget and device-spacing behavior; add no separate allowance or fairness system. Known unsupported targets are blocked before sending; retain typed sender not-sent results when encountered. Other actions continue. Command actions still run during quiet hours. Leave the existing daily quiet-hours implementation intact; no shared weekly compiler or new timezone logic.
- **Results and run-now.** Extend the existing bounded automation log for attempted actions and admission outcomes: occurrence/action/target, receipt or typed failure, blocked/skipped/busy. Preserve event data and exclude non-moment outcomes from flourish budgets. No additional history store. Run-now returns its occurrence ID within the HTTP bound; eventual per-action results come from the existing log, without resubmitting the run. Creating, editing, enabling and running need existing control authority for every affected target; proposals stay disabled until owner approval.

**Dependencies:** https://github.com/jimmie-potts/agent-device-hub/issues/358 and https://github.com/jimmie-potts/agent-device-hub/issues/335 are delivered at source level. https://github.com/jimmie-potts/agent-device-hub/issues/67 still supplies desk presets. https://github.com/jimmie-potts/divoom-app-upgrade/issues/13 supplies atomic Pixoo mode admission; current commands may use the snapshot fallback first. Its new rendition operation also needs https://github.com/jimmie-potts/divoom-app-upgrade/issues/96 and has no equivalent fallback. Do not implement these providers here or claim their unfinished actions delivered. https://github.com/jimmie-potts/agent-device-hub/issues/381 later reuses the executor; its event pairing and palette resolution are excluded.

### Behavior and protections to preserve

- One authoritative hub owner and one writer per device through the owning controller, with existing authentication, origin/header checks, queues and admission guards.
- No unapproved target, implicit mode takeover, automatic replay or retry. `sent` remains transport evidence, not proof of visible output.
- Existing event rules, settings and log data survive the schema change. Use one deliberate forward migration and document downgrade limitations; no automatic rollback framework.
- Keep the current released-state migration exclusion for automation data. Host-migration tooling and live-state migration are outside this story.
- A hub or model outage does not blank the devices' base presentation. Credentials and tokens remain excluded from rules and results.

### Observable acceptance and planned evidence

Use focused tests with a controllable local clock and the existing fake controllers/sender. Extend existing suites; do not duplicate their protocol matrices.

- [ ] **AC1 — Local scheduling.** An enabled `{days,time}` schedule selects the expected weekday and local minute, continues to its next occurrence, and recomputes after an edit. Disabling/deleting a pending rule prevents dispatch. No zone field, timezone dependency, custom DST handling, timezone-change test or cross-zone matrix is required.
- [ ] **AC2 — No catch-up.** After downtime spanning scheduled times, restart sends nothing for them and writes no missed-history entries. The next future occurrence runs once; a duplicate occurrence sends nothing twice. Staging/shutdown/release prevents new dispatch, including after a pending read. Do not add long-outage reconstruction or clock-change simulation suites.
- [ ] **AC3 — Guarded ordered execution.** A short action list uses fresh guards and runs in order; one offline/failed action permits the next one, with truthful results and no retry. Overlap returns `busy`. A valid content-mode action runs; a disallowed or unconfirmed required mode and an unauthorized target produce zero command writes. A manual change is superseded by the next occurrence without needing a manual-history row.
- [ ] **AC4 — Scheduled moments.** A fake capable target receives one arbitrated flourish per moment action with `coversStatus:false`. Distinct actions have distinct identities. Existing quiet-hours/Quiet and unsupported-target blocks remain visible while other actions continue. Reuse existing arbitration/sender tests for detailed switch, budget, negotiation and receipt behavior; add only the routine integration coverage and ensure command/skip/busy rows do not count as flourishes.
- [ ] **AC5 — Persistence and run-now.** Existing event rules/logs and new routines survive one close/reopen after the schema change. Run-now checks all target authority and the busy rule, answers within the HTTP bound with its own occurrence ID, and exposes eventual results in the bounded log. Running now does not consume the next scheduled occurrence. No missed-run or manual-command history is collected.
- [ ] **AC6 — Delivery.** Issue-linked OpenSpec delta, applicable existing hub/shared checks, two independent Standards and Specification reviews, and current-head/merged-revision CI. Keep a concise evidence map. No endurance run, exhaustive device/timezone/failure matrix, new benchmark, extra specialist review by default, or live hardware trial is required for source delivery.

**Delivery target:** source-only. Installing/enabling this on the owner's hub and any physical run remain separately authorized. A later practical acceptance can run one Pixoo playlist routine in Media, then confirm it skips in Monitor; this is not a source-delivery prerequisite.

### Meaningful deferrals

- **Timezone selection/conversion and custom DST or zone-change rules:** https://github.com/jimmie-potts/agent-device-hub/issues/674. Current schedules follow the host's local clock. Revisit only when the owner needs a schedule independent of that clock; no support or qualification for that behavior is claimed now.
- **Missed-run and manual-command history:** https://github.com/jimmie-potts/agent-device-hub/issues/675. Downtime leaves no missed ledger or completeness claim. Use run-now explicitly if needed; absence of a log row does not prove a past run succeeded.
- **One-off dates, ranges, holidays, suspension and additional conditions:** unchanged deferrals. Enable/disable by hand; music precedence remains https://github.com/jimmie-potts/agent-device-hub/issues/40.
- **UI and MCP:** https://github.com/jimmie-potts/agent-device-hub/issues/360. Until then use the typed routes.
- **Broader history, coordinated looks and future device moments:** https://github.com/jimmie-potts/agent-device-hub/issues/282, https://github.com/jimmie-potts/agent-device-hub/issues/267, https://github.com/jimmie-potts/agent-device-hub/issues/297 and https://github.com/jimmie-potts/agent-device-hub/issues/337 keep their own scope; none becomes a new prerequisite here.

### Work assessment

Owner-approved planning reassessment, September 30, 2026, against main `299a86ff709f1d842e874c39b846478a53f405ae` and the live related issues. One operator, one existing installation and explicitly configured controllers.

- **Complexity: medium.** A bounded local timer and executor still cross persistence and guarded device operations, but timezone compilation, missed-history accounting, manual auditing, migration tooling and broad test matrices are removed.
- **Uncertainty: low for the selected scheduling policy.** Final desk-preset and rendition integrations depend on their owning providers. These dependencies do not justify rebuilding them here.
- **Impact: medium.** Unattended device changes retain target authority, mode checks, bounded work, no replay/retry and truthful results.

**Readiness:** #358/#335 no longer block source work. Existing-action and scheduled-moment work can proceed under this definition; the full accepted action set still needs its named providers. Keep backlog status until delivery is selected and those action dependencies are reconciled. Deferred timezone/history work never blocks this story. Reassess for a different host-clock requirement, an action-provider change, or a repeated observed failure.

**Policy update (2026-09-25):** the owner retired the rule that kept titles, project names, prompts, transcripts and paths out of shared data (#424). Credentials and tokens stay excluded. This story's text was updated to match.

issues.body:

issues.title: Keep the now-playing displays working when the selected playback source changes
issues.body:
### Outcome and real setup

The Tidbyt now-playing tile and the Pixoo card from [#38](https://github.com/jimmie-potts/agent-device-hub/issues/38) keep showing what is playing when the owner switches the hub's selected playback source. The trigger is [#301](https://github.com/jimmie-potts/agent-device-hub/issues/301), which adds the Sonos Move as a selectable source.

Today both displays pin `sourceId: "ht-a9"`: the Tidbyt runner's `nowPlaying` block and the Pixoo's `agent-monitor/playback.json`. Both read with credentials whose `devices` list only `ht-a9`. Each display also rejects a snapshot for any other source ID as a failed read. So once the Move is selected, the hub answers 403 and the displays show nothing after 30 s, with no error the owner can see.

Setup: one operator, the installed hub, the Tidbyt runner inside the local controller host from #318, and the Pixoo user service.

### Smallest useful implementation

Pick one when this is defined:

- **(a)** Documented reconfiguration: when the selected source changes, update both display configurations and both credentials' `devices`, then restart the host and the Pixoo service.
- **(b)** Let each display follow the hub's selected source. It would accept whatever `sourceId` the snapshot names, with credentials listing every configured source.

(b) needs a decision, because the strict source check was deliberate: it stops a display from showing another source's music. An unavailable selected source must still show as unavailable (see the architecture's Shared playback section).
